To express your opinion with varied formulas (en mi opinión, desde mi punto de vista, estoy convencido de que).
To use estar a favor / en contra de que + SUBJUNCTIVE.

October. Rosa Elena is nearly three and goes to a nursery in the neighbourhood. Her teacher, Mrs Radu, has asked to see Ana: she’s worried that the little girl mixes Romanian and Spanish. The nursery head speaks Spanish.
Ms García, thank you for coming. The teacher is worried. She says Rosa Elena mixes up the languages. Yesterday she asked for “un pahar de agua”.
I understand your concern. However, from my point of view, it’s completely normal in a bilingual child.
Maybe. But the teacher thinks it would be better if you only spoke Romanian at home, at least until she starts school.
With all due respect, I don’t agree that that would be best. The studies say the opposite: children who grow up with two languages separate them on their own at around four.
You’re right that there are many studies. But here most of the children only speak Romanian. We’re worried Rosa Elena might feel different.
It’s true that she’s different. But it’s not that it’s a problem; it’s an opportunity. For her and for the other children.
I’m in favour of the children learning that other languages exist. I could come once a month and tell them a story in Spanish. Free of charge, of course.
Mmm… That’s an interesting idea. Although I think some parents will be against another language being taught so early.
I understand. That’s why I suggest we discuss it at the parents’ meeting. If most of them don’t want it, I won’t insist.
That seems fair to me. But tell me one thing, as a mother: aren’t you afraid your daughter won’t speak either of the two languages well?

Honestly, no. My husband learned Spanish as an adult, and I’m learning Romanian. She’s had them since the cradle. All in all, the important thing is that she’s happy and feels at home in both countries.
Very well, Ms García. You’ve convinced me. Well, almost. We’ll discuss it at the meeting.
“desde mi punto de vista” = from my point of view
“estar de acuerdo con” = to agree with
“tener razón en que” = to be right that
“no es que… sino que” = it’s not that… but that
“a favor de que” = in favour of
Pause after connectors: «Es cierto que…, | pero…». «Desde mi punto de vista, | …». The pauses make your argument sound calm and confident.
kon-TO-do-el-rres-PEH-to: the polite formula before you contradict someone. Your tone should be calm, not aggressive.
bee-LEEN-gweh: “ü” (with two dots) is pronounced “w”: bee-leen-GWEH. Without the dots it would be “bee-leen-geh”.
En mi opinión, / Desde mi punto de vista,
No creo que / No me parece que
Vary your formulas! A text that starts every sentence with “creo que” sounds A2. Alternate: en mi opinión, desde mi punto de vista, estoy convencido de que.
When you’re for or against an action by SOMEONE ELSE, the structure takes the SUBJUNCTIVE (it’s a wish / assessment, as in chapter 38):
Estoy a favor de que los niños hablen dos idiomas.
Estoy en contra de fumar en los bares.
Estoy en contra de que se fume en los bares.
No estoy de acuerdo con que eso sea un problema.
Me parece injusto que la juzguen por eso.
“Estoy de acuerdo en que” + INDICATIVE (you agree with a fact): Estoy de acuerdo en que es difícil. But “No estoy de acuerdo con que” + SUBJUNCTIVE.
The strongest argument first acknowledges what the other person is right about, then counters it. It sounds mature and polite:
Es cierto que los mezcla, pero es normal.
Tiene(s) razón en que…; sin embargo, …
Tiene razón en que hay riesgos; sin embargo, …
Puede que sea difícil, pero vale la pena.
Aunque es diferente, eso no es un problema.
“Puede que” takes the subjunctive (chapter 39), “es cierto que” takes the indicative (it states a fact).
To correct a wrong idea: NO ES QUE + subjunctive (the idea you reject), SINO QUE + indicative (the right idea):
It’s not that it’s a problem; it’s an opportunity.
It’s not that I don’t want to help you; I just don’t have time.
It’s one of B1–B2 examiners’ favourite structures. Use it once in every argumentative text!

An article from the expat magazine: two parents with opposing views.

For. Laura, a Spanish mother in Cluj: “I’m convinced that speaking two languages from an early age is a gift. It’s true that at first children mix them up, but by around four they separate them perfectly.”
“Besides, studies show that bilingual children are more mentally flexible. It’s not that they’re more intelligent; it’s that they adapt better to change.”

Against. Andrés, a father in Timișoara: “From my point of view, it’s better for a child to master one language properly before learning another. My son started talking very late and I think it was because of the confusion.”
“Those who say it’s an advantage in the long term are right; however, I think it’s unfair to put pressure on parents to do it. Each family should decide.”
All in all, they both agree on one thing: the important thing is for a child to feel loved. In any language.
“a largo plazo” = in the long term

¿Qué le pasó al hijo de Andrés?
¿En qué están de acuerdo los dos?

The parents’ meeting took place on a Thursday afternoon, in the nursery’s biggest room. The chairs were tiny and colourful, designed for three-year-olds. The parents sat on them with their knees up to their chins.

There were about twenty of them. Ana knew some by sight: the twins’ mother, the father who was always late, the grandmother who picked up her granddaughter every day with a bag of covrigi. Mihai had taken the afternoon off from the hospital and was sitting next to her, on a green chair that creaked every time he moved.
The head explained the proposal in Romanian: once a month, a Spanish mother would tell the children a story in Spanish. It would be voluntary, free and only twenty minutes.
At first nobody said anything. Then a bearded father raised his hand. Mihai whispered a translation to Ana.

“He says that, with all due respect, he’s against it. That the children have enough on their plate learning Romanian properly. That his daughter still says ‘cocoloș’ instead of ‘cocoș’ and he doesn’t want to confuse her any further.”

Other parents nodded. One mother added that she thought it was unfair to teach only Spanish: why not English, which is more useful? Another said that if a foreign language was going to be taught, she wanted it to be French, because her husband was from Lyon.
Within five minutes the meeting had turned into a little chaos. Everyone was talking at once. The head was trying, unsuccessfully, to restore order. Ana looked at Mihai, discouraged.

Then the grandmother with the covrigi stood up. She was a small woman of about seventy, with a flowery headscarf. She waited for everyone to fall silent. And when there was finally silence, she spoke slowly.
“I was born in a village on the Hungarian border. At home, my mother spoke Romanian and my father Hungarian. My grandmother spoke German. Nobody ever thought that was a problem. It was just life.”

“It’s true that, as a little girl, I mixed them up. My mother laughed because I said made-up words, half Romanian and half Hungarian. But by five I spoke all three. And during the war, when soldiers came from everywhere, I was the one who translated for the whole village.”
“It’s not that learning languages makes children cleverer. It’s that it opens doors for them. Doors that we grown-ups sometimes don’t even know exist.”
Nobody said anything. The bearded father was looking at the floor. The mother who wanted French had her arms crossed, but she no longer looked so annoyed.
Then the grandmother did something nobody expected. She turned to Ana and spoke to her directly, in slow but correct Spanish:

“Madam, I’m in favour of you coming to tell stories. But on one condition: next month, the French father comes. And then the mother who wants English. And I, if you’ll let me, will tell them a story in Hungarian. That way the children will know the world is big.”
Ana was left speechless. Mihai looked at her, surprised. “You speak Spanish?” he asked her.
The grandmother smiled. “A little bit. I go to the Instituto Cervantes on Tuesdays. My teacher’s name is Ana García.” And she winked at Ana.

It took Ana a few seconds to recognise her. Without the bun, without the round glasses and with that flowery headscarf, she looked like a different person. It was Mrs Ecaterina, García Márquez’s translator. Her granddaughter went to the same nursery as Rosa Elena. She had never told her.

The vote was quick. Eighteen parents in favour, two against. One of the two who voted against was the bearded father. But on the way out, he came up to Ana and told her, in very simple English, that maybe next year he’d change his mind.
It was already dark in the street. Ana and Mihai walked home slowly under the neighbourhood’s bare acacias.
“You know what’s funniest?” said Ana. “I’d prepared ten arguments. Studies, figures, examples. And in the end, a grandmother with a bag of covrigi convinced them.”
“She didn’t convince them with arguments,” Mihai answered. “She convinced them with a story. Like you always do in class.”
A month later, Ana sat on one of the nursery’s tiny chairs, in front of twenty three-year-olds. Rosa Elena was in the front row, very serious, with her hands on her knees.

Ana opened a picture book. It wasn’t a bought book. It was a sketchbook Andrei had made during the summer: the story of a white cat who travelled from Bucharest to Madrid and from Madrid to Tokyo, and in every city learned to say “hello” in a different way.
“Once upon a time there was a cat called Tudor…” Ana began, in Spanish.
The children stared at her open-mouthed. They understood almost nothing. But when the cat reached Madrid and said “¡Hola!”, twenty little voices repeated it at once: “¡Hola!”
And Rosa Elena, from the front row, shouted louder than anyone, in her three languages at once: “¡Hola! Bună! Konnichiwa!”

At the back of the room, sitting on a chair far too small for her, Mrs Ecaterina wiped away a tear with the corner of her headscarf. And she thought that maybe, after all, she had translated the right book.

In the months that followed, Mrs Ecaterina’s idea came true exactly. In November the French father came; he turned out to be a chef and told a story about a mouse who stole cheese in Paris. The children said “fromage” for a whole week.
In December the mother who wanted English came. She brought a guitar and sang carols. The head was so delighted that she sang along, even though she sang terribly out of tune.

In January it was Mrs Ecaterina’s turn. In Hungarian, she told the story of an enchanted stag that guided two brothers to a new land. Not one child understood a word, but they all sat still, listening, as if it were the voice of a real grandmother. And it was.

And in February, surprisingly, the bearded father raised his hand. He had prepared a story in Romanian, but with a new word on every page: one in Spanish, one in French, one in English, one in Hungarian.
When he finished, his daughter stood up and, very proudly, said all the new words in a row. At the end, to finish off, she said “cocoloș”. All the parents burst out laughing. He laughed first.

That evening, at home, Rosa Elena didn’t want to go to sleep. She wanted Ana to tell her the story of Tudor the cat again. And then the one about the mouse in Paris. And then the one about the enchanted stag.
“Mummy,” she asked at the end, half asleep, in a perfect mix of Romanian and Spanish, “are all the stories in the world true?”

Ana thought of Grandma Rosario and Andrés’s bread, of Grandpa Gheorghe and the white she-bear, of the box under the floor. “Yes, my love,” she answered. “They’re all true. You just have to know which language to listen to them in.”

Text to read: The bearded father’s letter
A month later, the father who voted against sends Ana a letter.
Dear Ms García: I am writing to tell you something I find hard to admit. I voted against your proposal. Today I think I was wrong.
On the day of the story, my daughter came home saying “¡Hola!” to everyone: me, her mother, the dog and the postman.
It’s not that she suddenly speaks Spanish; it’s that now she’s curious about everything. She asks me how to say every single thing in other languages.
It’s true that she still says “cocoloș”. But, all in all, I agree that children should discover that the world is big. Yours sincerely, the bearded father.
A todo el mundo, incluso al perro
